name: Leaf
lede: Leaf is a fresh, strong yellow-green, the color a young leaf shows against the light; the same word in older color lists names the brown of a dead one.

sections.title: Two leaves, two colors
sections.body:
The swatch comes from a 2010 survey and sits closest to the ISCC-NBS block called strong yellow green, 5.9 units away [11]. Its nearest neighbors in our data are [[leaf]], [[grass]] and [[leaf-green]] [11]. The older name lists point the other way: the ISCC-NBS record of the name *leaf* sits in block 51, whose other names are Autumn Leaf, Dead Leaf, Feuille Morte and Leaf Brown [11]. Block 51 is an orange-brown block, nothing like this green [11]. The color word has always carried both ends of a leaf's year.

Paterson's dictionary of colour shows the same split. Leaf green is the color of leaves, sometimes the yellowy green of young leaves, and one of the colors in the Ostwald circle [4]. *Feuille* alone is a light green, but *feuillemorte* is the brown of dead leaves, spelled in many ways, among them filemot and philamot [4]. Leafmold is a dark reddish-orange, and dead-leaf brown has an entry of its own [4]. The dictionary also records that *chlorosis* has two opposite meanings: a leaf turning green from some other color, or a leaf lacking chlorophyll and turning yellow or white [4].

sections.title: Why a leaf is green
sections.body:
The green of a leaf comes from chlorophyll, which Paterson describes as the substance held in the tiny bodies called chloroplasts in plant cells [4]. What we see is also a matter of how the eye compares cone signals. Livingstone observes that a leaf, an orange and a tomato look green, orange and red under both daylight and office fluorescents, even though a spectrophotometer shows big differences [7]. What defines their color is the ratio of long to middle cone signals, which rises from the leaf to the orange to the tomato [7]. Westland adds a practical point for painters and photographers: light shining through a translucent leaf heightens its chroma [8].

Green is not the color plants use best. Birren describes older experiments in which wheat grew best under red rays, with a fall-off under yellow and green and a pickup under blue [9]. Plant stems also lean toward a light source, because the shaded side grows faster [9].

sections.title: How painters get a leaf right
sections.body:
Gurney, writing for painters, breaks the light on a leaf into four kinds [2]. Transmitted light, with the sun behind the leaf, gives a strongly chromatic yellow-green [2]. A leaf in shadow, facing down, is the darkest green, even darker if it were not picking up reflected light from a neighbor [2]. A leaf in shadow, facing up, turns blue-green because the sky is shining on it [2]. Sunlight on the top surface gives the lightest and most textured color, but with a surprisingly weak chroma, because most of the light bounces off the waxy surface of the leaf [2].

This swatch is a transmitted-light green. On a whole tree, Gurney adds, the four kinds of foliage color mix like tiny pixels, grouped by how each mass of leaves faces the light [2]. His working advice is to vary the greens from leaf to leaf and tree to tree [3]. He also suggests weaving pink or reddish gray through them, and priming the canvas pink or red so that it shows through in places, a method he credits to the painter Stapleton Kearns as smuggling reds [3].

In our archive, [[painter:paul-gauguin|Gauguin]]'s [[painting:commons-Q79790701|Mother and Child under a Tree at Pont-Aven]] has the most of this green, at 31 per cent of the canvas, and Van Gogh's [[painting:nga-163323|Green Wheat Fields, Auvers]] has about a sixth [12].

sections.title: Autumn and the leaf study
sections.body:
Albers thought autumn foliage nowhere more brilliant than in the United States, and he built an exercise on it [5]. Students collect leaves, press and dry them, and use them alongside color paper, since leaves offer modulations and shapes that paper does not have [5]. The rule he sets is to keep the color before the shape in mind [5]. Fall leaf studies are best done in season; out of season, preserved leaves give more subdued, less vivid colors [5].

This is a good way to learn leaf as a color word. One leaf can be green at the stem, yellow-green at the edge, and orange-brown at the tip in the same week, and each part belongs to a different name in the dictionaries above.

sections.title: The leaf as a badge
sections.body:
On July 12, 1789, in the garden of the Palais-Royal, the lawyer Camille Desmoulins asked a crowd to choose a color for a cockade [10]. The crowd answered green, the symbol of hope, and he tore a leaf from a linden to pin to his hat [10]. Green ribbons soon replaced the leaves, but the next day the patriots learned that green was also the color of the detested Comte d'Artois, and the badge was reconsidered [10]. On July 14 those who stormed the Bastille wore a variety of colors, among them green, blue, red and combinations of them [10].

Pastoureau notes the same tree in an older story: in the Nibelungen legend, a fallen linden leaf left a spot on Siegfried's shoulders where the dragon's blood did not reach, so that he was not completely invulnerable [13].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
In our archive of 23,781 paintings, as photographed, the swatch fills five per cent of the canvas or more, within six units, in five [12]. They are Gauguin's *Pont-Aven* (31 per cent of it), Van Gogh's *Green Wheat Fields, Auvers* from 1890 (16 per cent) and Gauguin's 1888 self-portrait (13 per cent) [12]. The other two are an 1861 *Civil War Battle* (12 per cent) and Jawlensky's *Red Path, St. Prex* from 1915 (9 per cent) [12]. That is rarer than 82 per cent of named colors, and photographs of aged, varnished paintings are not pigment tests [12].

The closest gem in our data is [[gem:peridot|peridot]], a deeper olive, 9.4 units away [11]. The closest year-color is Pantone's Greenery, the Color of the Year for 2017, at 7.4 units [11]. In printed English, *leaf* as a color adjective rose fastest in the 1880s and peaked in the 1920s [14]. When you next look at a tree, find the four kinds of leaf on Gurney's list [2]. The transmitted yellow-green is the one closest to this swatch [2][11].

questions.q: Where does a leaf look most strongly chromatic yellow-green, according to Gurney?
choices: When light shines through it from behind
In direct sunlight on its top surface
When it faces the sky in shade
questions.answer: When light shines through it from behind

questions.q: What does the older name *feuille morte* describe?
True or false: the sunlit top surface of a leaf is the most intensely colored part.

openers: The word leaf names both the green of spring and, in older color lists, the brown of a dead one.
Look at a tree against the sun: the leaves lit from behind are the strongest yellow-green on it.
